solution_evidence_candidates.text:
@davidemannone: Unfortunately there are still a lot of breaking changes happening in ROS2, Nav2, Gazebo etc. on a regular basis, so expect some manual fiddling for a few days to avoid segfaults, but the good news is that usually there is a way to get stuff to run with enough persistence.

For instance you might need to export `QT_QPA_PLATFORM=xcb` to hamper Gazebo from crashing in case you are running in a VM, since Gazebo (other than simulators like Webots) is not smart enough to select a working graphics mode by itself or to give meaningful error messages for crashes.

Also Ubuntu Mesa drivers can cause issues in case you are using Ubuntu 24 already. This fixed the Mesa issue for me:

```
sudo add-apt-repository ppa:kisak/kisak-mesa
sudo apt update
sudo apt upgrade

```

Additionally you may need to pass some additional parameters. While this contradicts the tutorials, that's what at least seems to be needed for Jazzy to have the relevant nodes spawned up:

```
export QT_QPA_PLATFORM=xcb
ros2 launch nav2_bringup tb3_simulation_launch.py slam:=True nav:=True headless:=False use_sim_time:=True
```

Please let me know how that goes for you, if it doesn't work I am willing to share a VM file with you.

So, it looks like our Getting Started (and build/install) guide needs to be updated from the migration to New-Gazebo from Gazebo-Classic. Jazzy / Rolling don't have support for Gazebo Classic anymore since it doesn't ship with those distributions on 24.04. 

We are no longer dependent on the TB3 packages and instead use this repo instead for the URDFs and sim files https://github.com/ros-navigation/nav2_minimal_turtlebot_simulation. That step is not required to `apt install` anything other than packages in the minimal Tb3/4 repo -- which have binaries in Jazzy that you can use. The setting of the Gazebo model paths are also not required anymore (we automated that in the launch files).

Everything else should be the same. If you're open to contributing, I'd love it if you could propose the changes to that instruction set that aligns with the current state of the project using the modern updated gazebo! If nothing else, verifying that the changes i described above are the only changes required would be good and then I can make the updates myself when I have a spare few hours in the airport on the way to ROSCon :-)

For instance you might need to export `QT_QPA_PLATFORM=xcb` to hamper Gazebo from crashing in case you are running in a VM, since Gazebo (other than simulators like Webots) is not smart enough to select a working graphics mode by itself or to give meaningful error messages for crashes.

Also Ubuntu Mesa drivers can cause issues in case you are using Ubuntu 24 already. This fixed the Mesa issue for me:

```

- Processes still running in the background, make sure Gazebo and Rviz processes are fully gone before relaunching your stuff, there might also be potentially stuck ROS2 nodes. To test that easily you could logout and login again instead of a full restart. (though this doesn't exclude the next point, you will need to look at the concrete processes to distinguish)

- It could be an issue with your graphics driver (open source drivers often have strange bugs): `export LIBGL_ALWAYS_SOFTWARE=1` (in addition to export `QT_QPA_PLATFORM=xcb`) will switch to more stable but slow CPU-based rendering. Thank you for your detailed output. It seems very similar to what I experienced. It probably means for now the sensor simulation needs to happen on the CPU. However chances are very good that you can have GPU acceleration with Gazebo if it is fine for you to run sdf files with lower graphics requirements. Here is a command you can try which might allow you to run GPU-accelerated Gazebo for visualization, with CPU-based sensor simulation, which should work repeatedly:

```
export MY_WORLD=/opt/ros/jazzy/share/nav2_minimal_tb4_sim/worlds/warehouse.sdf
export QT_QPA_PLATFORM=xcb
export LIBGL_ALWAYS_SOFTWARE=1
gnome-terminal -- bash -c "sleep 10 && export LIBGL_ALWAYS_SOFTWARE=0 && export QT_QPA_PLATFORM=xcb && gz sim --render-engine ogre \$MY_WORLD; exec bash" &
ros2 launch nav2_bringup tb4_simulation_launch.py slam:=True nav:=True headless:=True autostart:=True use_sim_time:=True rviz_config_file:=nartech_view.rviz world:=$MY_WORLD
```

## Bug report

**Required Info:**

- Operating System:
  - Ubuntu 24.04
- ROS2 Version:
  - Jazzy / Rolling

```bash
ros2 launch nav2_bringup tb3_simulation_launch.py headless:=False use_rviz:=False

Rviz has no relationship with Nav2 in terms of functional performance. However, as the [Getting Started Guide](https://docs.nav2.org/getting_started/index.html) mentions, you need to give the robot its initial pose on startup so that you can complete the map->odom->base_link transformation tree. You do that in tutorial / testing using rviz, though in production its based on the known robot's last pose. If you didn't have rviz launch, then you probably didn't set this initial pose, and thus you see the global costmap timing out.

tl;dr: you need to set the initial pose. You can see this done in all Nav2 system tests, Nav2 python simple commander demos, and in other tutorial/educational demonstrations of Nav2 on GitHub :-)

Thanks for reporting @evshary 

I'll take a look at it soon.

I know you've got a few things on your queue @padhupradheep for Nav2 -- I'd put this on the bottom, the other 2 are higher priority. This is something we should fix for sure, but isn't functionally breaking Nav2 uses in deployed applications, so I would deprioritize this over those 

If @evshary or another user wants to jump in to debug further, I'm sure we'd appreciate it!

Did a very quick dig, seems to be that for some reason, when https://github.com/ros-navigation/navigation2/blob/90a6c8d80096469a22e1a56e5447d58fb8e66ef6/nav2_rviz_plugins/src/selector.cpp#L158 the plugin loader is called here in the above line and when the `get_parameters` function is called here: https://github.com/ros-navigation/navigation2/blob/90a6c8d80096469a22e1a56e5447d58fb8e66ef6/nav2_rviz_plugins/src/utils.cpp#L53 for some reason we have to wait few minutes for the function to return the parameters. This never occurred here https://github.com/ros-navigation/navigation2/blob/90a6c8d80096469a22e1a56e5447d58fb8e66ef6/nav2_rviz_plugins/src/selector.cpp#L156

This is weird to see the `SyncParametersClient` taking that much time to return the `planner_plugins`. I'm not sure if this issue is also there in Iron. Need to check it once.

That is odd, considering that the controller is actually activated before the planner https://github.com/ros-navigation/navigation2/blob/main/nav2_bringup/launch/navigation_launch.py#L44

Might be better to have it do this update in a separate thread so that it doesn't block bringup -  then update its values once you have them. We could also do an async param get and after some timeout retry once so that if there's some discovery issues we try again once things have calmed down
Makes sense to me. @evshary you want to give a swing at it?
Hi @padhupradheep Thanks for looking into it. I could give it a try, but I've been blocked with other issues currently. Therefore, don't wait for me if this is urgent.

title: MPPI GoalCritic and Path Inversion Bug

fault_phenomenon.title: MPPI GoalCritic and Path Inversion Bug
fault_phenomenon.description:
## Bug report

**Required Info:**

- Operating System:
  - ubuntu 24.04
- Computer:
  - 13th Gen Intel NUC
- ROS2 Version:
  - Jazzy
- Version or commit hash:
  - main repository
- DDS implementation:
  - Fast-RTPS

#### Steps to reproduce issue
The MPPI controller's GoalCritic behavior, modified in PR #4822, causes the robot to ignore local path inversions and focus solely on the global goal.

1. Set up a Nav2 environment with the MPPI controller.
2. Create a path with an inversion point (e.g., in a narrow aisle requiring a 180-degree turn).
3. Send a goal pose with an orientation opposite to the robot's current direction.
4. Observe the robot bypassing the inversion point and moving directly to the final goal.

#### Expected behavior
The robot should respect path inversions, navigating to intermediary goals (e.g., inversion points) when required, before approaching the final goal.

#### Actual behavior
The robot to ignore local path inversions and focus solely on the global goal.

#### Additional information
Proposed Solution:
Default to using the "real" (global) goal for GoalCritic scoring and other critics.

If a path inversion is detected and inversions are considered (based on a parameter), use the intermediary goal (end of the pruned path or inversion point).

solution_evidence_candidates.text: @BriceRenaudeau reverting #4822 would reintroduce the bug that it solved :) Instead, you could open a PR with the solution that @SteveMacenski suggested.

comments.body:

Anyone in the community open to helping with this? It involves adding the parameter for enforcing path inversions and using the global goal pose vs the path's end pose considering path inversions when MPPI is used with a feasible planner like Smac Planner Hybrid-A*.

The quickest solution is to revert the faulty MR #4822
@BriceRenaudeau reverting #4822 would reintroduce the bug that it solved :) Instead, you could open a PR with the solution that @SteveMacenski suggested.

I've also marked it with help-wanted. I've been noticing many of these tickets have had community members jump in to help too, so I've been leaving nice bite-sized things like this open for them to contribute and grow. If this isn't something @BriceRenaudeau @alex-roba @redvinaa can do, at some point I'll address it myself but wanted to give open opportunity to the community to be involved before I did.

I'd like to take a closer look and work on a definitive fix so that the MPPI controller can be used reliably. If you're okay with it, I’ll go ahead and start working on this.

title: Bug in parameter configuration in controller.

fault_phenomenon.title: Bug in parameter configuration in controller.
fault_phenomenon.description:
I think I have found a bug related to parameter configuration in the controller. 

I started the robot as usual this morning and it gave me this configuration error on startup.

![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/0e627c6c-0430-4a35-a16e-4e27f773b73a)

It says that ``The value of parameter 'MPPI.vx_min' is incorrectly set to -0.350000, it should be >=0. Ignoring parameter update.``.

I looked at the documentation and this is the  default value: https://docs.nav2.org/configuration/packages/configuring-mppic.html

I also looked at this part of the code and I found it in the RPP controller!!! 

https://github.com/ros-navigation/navigation2/blob/5423eba732ed16b4f97a7353027c1f444b6edc60/nav2_regulated_pure_pursuit_controller/src/parameter_handler.cpp#L230-L234

Maybe this is related to this PR #4971

error_logs.text: I started the robot as usual this morning and it gave me this configuration error on startup.

comments.body:
I ... am getting annoyed by the dynamic parameter APIs. 

Here's what we do. Check if the parameter name starts with `plugin_name_`. If it doesn't, then `continue` in the loop. That way we skip any non-this-plugin parameters set. 

Heck, that might also be the solution for MPPI with the non-MPPI parameter changes triggering resets we've been talking about over Slack. Lets do that in MPPI too. 

Then, we can rearrange this ticket to updating all Plugins to do the same, since all plugin's parameters are or should be under the plugin's root namespace. I think this is a good global change.
@ajtudela Thank you for catching this. I indeed introduced this bug in #4971. Sry for that! This PR should hopefully fix it: #5106.

## Bug report

**Required Info:**

- Operating System:
  - Ubuntu 24.04
- Computer:
  - Thinkpad T480
- ROS2 Version:
  - Jazzy
- Version or commit hash:
  - 1.3.6-1noble.20250430.062618
- DDS implementation:
  - CycloneDDS

#### Steps to reproduce issue
- trigger action DockRobot on a charging dock (this succeeds)
- trigger action DockRobot the same charging dock (this fails)

#### Expected behavior
If the robot is already docked in the charging dock, and docking request should succeed without moving the robot. 

An alternative (more complex) behavior would be to return an error code that could then be used to determine if "already docked where you wanted" is a success or failure in whatever is calling the docking action.

#### Actual behavior
The robot fails to dock the second time.

#### Reproduction instructions
No special setup should be needed other than the robot must be considered docked when the 2nd DockRobot action is called.

#### Additional information

I am running into this on a custom subclass of ChargingDock, but the bug occurs before any custom code is run (in docking_server.cpp, which I'm not modifying).

The bug occurs here:
https://github.com/ros-navigation/navigation2/blob/main/nav2_docking/opennav_docking/src/docking_server.cpp#L252

IMO it's just an oversight where dockRobot() is returning without accounting for the fact that it's in an action handler callback and should succeed or fail the goal rather than just hanging up on the action client.

It might be sufficient to add:
```
result->success = true;
docking_action_server_->succeeded_current(result);
```

This bug's behavior is quite silly when translated to other contexts:

- Teacher: "Please do this week's homework assignment"
- Student: "I handed it in already!"
- Teacher: "You fail!"

## Issue 1: Refine Path Issue (Tentatively Completed)

I'm thinking @stevedanomodolor's PR solves the issue @wang-fire  brought up in https://github.com/ros-navigation/navigation2/issues/5188 and https://github.com/ros-navigation/navigation2/issues/5192#issuecomment-2911274182. @wang-fire can you review, test locally, and let us know if that resolves this element so you can use `humble_main` again? I believe that it should and an important incremental fix.

Edit: I merged https://github.com/ros-navigation/navigation2/pull/5198 after @stevedanomodolor said he was able to test briefly and couldn't reproduce it but would appreciate your final 👍 @wang-fire. I suspect this can be called _COMPLETED_ now

## Issue 2: Reeds-Shepp Single-Point Oddity (In Progress)

With respect to the single point issue in the original ticket, I can reproduce that on Jazzy myself when using the default parameters in the [Docs](https://docs.nav2.org/configuration/packages/smac/configuring-smac-hybrid.html) with the change of using the Reeds-Shepp model rather than Dubins (no issue with dubins). So, I don't think its just parameterizations. 

Update with development results 5:29pm PST: 

I'll spare you the convoluted details about how I got here, but I was able to log inside of the analytic expansion the directional turns that the reeds-shepp paths themselves generated and found that I was correct that it is the Reeds-Shepp paths legit have the extra backup-and-then-move-forward behavior. While most of the time I see it happen due to the turning radius refinement stage, I can also see it normally happen in the raw Reeds-Shepp path that is generated by OMPL as the shortest possible path. That is the legit, shortest path using Reeds-Shepp curves so that is technically correct behavior. 

Thus, this isn't strictly speaking a bug, this is intended behavior to have the shortest minimum turning radius path to the goal pose and orientation. Though, I fully ACK that this can be annoying or look like a bug. Possible suggestions (**any other suggestions?**):
- Do nothing, this is actually drivable and correct
- Limit the analytic expansion curve to be facing in the same direction of motion as the expansion it represents is in (i.e. forward primitive must start with forward, reverse primitive must start with reversing). While that would completely eliminate the possibility of a path like this, that would open up an edge case possibly in confined settings where this is strictly necessary to be able to find an exact route to the goal. I suppose it could be parameterized, however it doesn't prevent other reversing-type plans > 1 point long. 
- We could add in an additional refinement heuristic that prefers solutions with less directional changes, even if at the cost of a longer path and/or path closer to potential obstacles. That could eliminate some of them, but wouldn't make it impossible to happen
- We could add a constraint on the refinements so that it should not add any more directional changes than the original solution provides. If it does, then we consider it less optimal and don't consider it further, even if its shorter or in lower cost space. 

I think the last one is the best in my opinion.  I have a prototype in https://github.com/ros-navigation/navigation2/pull/5207 to test. If the shortest path by the turning radius really does involve doing that, maybe we should let it. However, if it happens due to refinements for cost weighting / increasing turning radius, perhaps we should prefer sticking with the original value (or another turning value that's not as extreme) which doesn't increase that count. That makes it still possible to happen, but only if its natural for it to happen and not due to later refinement. I'm finding that most of the time this happens is due to the refinement stage, so this would remove some big percentage of them. I also married it with a check to see if there's a refinement that is less than the original cost (but might be larger than some other refined cost) and uses less segments to use. If its better than original and less directional segments, I think that is the preferable direction over slightly shorter but having 2x direction changes. 

What does everyone think?

Specifically, a planner (I use the lattice one, humble_main branch) can sometimes generate an incorrect x (and possibly y) value in the goal pose, resulting in an entirely incorrect path to the another, not target, position. I tested reverting commit f5543c39aba5d3302208bc6e9696e7cbd41de8c9, and that resolved the problem. But I have no idea how is it possible. 

How can i reproduce this, what goals are you sending? I am not getting this behavior locally. Can you with this pr https://github.com/ros-navigation/navigation2/pull/5198 to see if you get the x and y issue. 
Also lets stick to one branch, the one with the fix, so we don't mix problems.

> How can i reproduce this, what goals are you sending?

I use diff platform with reverse_expansion, the footprint is rectangle. The goal is about 10m far away from robot. Not sure other details are important, because I don't use full nav2 stack. 
 

> Can you with this pr [#5198](https://github.com/ros-navigation/navigation2/pull/5198) to see if you get the x and y issue.

No, this fix does not treat my issue =(

> > How can i reproduce this, what goals are you sending?
> 
> I use diff platform with reverse_expansion, the footprint is rectangle. The goal is about 10m far away from robot. Not sure other details are important, because I don't use full nav2 stack. 
>  
> 
> > Can you with this pr [#5198](https://github.com/ros-navigation/navigation2/pull/5198) to see if you get the x and y issue.
> 
> No, this fix does not treat my issue =(

To prevent from mixing issues and given that your stack is not full nav2, while i work on understanding the initial issue with the path including backward and forward movement, i recommend you look and log into the input that gets sent to the planners. You can find this here  https://github.com/ros-navigation/navigation2/blob/1278df713a4fa4e80cc6d5903046180ec3b3686b/nav2_smac_planner/src/smac_planner_hybrid.cpp#L449.

The x y, seem to be an issue that would be quite noticeable when it happens and i have not seen it happen.

Maybe @SteveMacenski has more insight on the x y issue.

## Issue 1: Refine Path Issue (Tentatively Completed)

I'm thinking @stevedanomodolor's PR solves the issue @wang-fire  brought up in https://github.com/ros-navigation/navigation2/issues/5188 and https://github.com/ros-navigation/navigation2/issues/5192#issuecomment-2911274182. @wang-fire can you review, test locally, and let us know if that resolves this element so you can use `humble_main` again? I believe that it should and an important incremental fix.

Edit: I merged https://github.com/ros-navigation/navigation2/pull/5198 after @stevedanomodolor said he was able to test briefly and couldn't reproduce it but would appreciate your final 👍 @wang-fire. I suspect this can be called _COMPLETED_ now

## Issue 2: Reeds-Shepp Single-Point Oddity (In Progress)

With respect to the single point issue in the original ticket, I can reproduce that on Jazzy myself when using the default parameters in the [Docs](https://docs.nav2.org/configuration/packages/smac/configuring-smac-hybrid.html) with the change of using the Reeds-Shepp model rather than Dubins (no issue with dubins). So, I don't think its just parameterizations. 

Update with development results 5:29pm PST: 

I'll spare you the convoluted details about how I got here, but I was able to log inside of the analytic expansion the directional turns that the reeds-shepp paths themselves generated and found that I was correct that it is the Reeds-Shepp paths legit have the extra backup-and-then-move-forward behavior. While most of the time I see it happen due to the turning radius refinement stage, I can also see it normally happen in the raw Reeds-Shepp path that is generated by OMPL as the shortest possible path. That is the legit, shortest path using Reeds-Shepp curves so that is technically correct behavior. 

Thus, this isn't strictly speaking a bug, this is intended behavior to have the shortest minimum turning radius path to the goal pose and orientation. Though, I fully ACK that this can be annoying or look like a bug. Possible suggestions (**any other suggestions?**):
- Do nothing, this is actually drivable and correct
- Limit the analytic expansion curve to be facing in the same direction of motion as the expansion it represents is in (i.e. forward primitive must start with forward, reverse primitive must start with reversing). While that would completely eliminate the possibility of a path like this, that would open up an edge case possibly in confined settings where this is strictly necessary to be able to find an exact route to the goal. I suppose it could be parameterized, however it doesn't prevent other reversing-type plans > 1 point long. 
- We could add in an additional refinement heuristic that prefers solutions with less directional changes, even if at the cost of a longer path and/or path closer to potential obstacles. That could eliminate some of them, but wouldn't make it impossible to happen
- We could add a constraint on the refinements so that it should not add any more directional changes than the original solution provides. If it does, then we consider it less optimal and don't consider it further, even if its shorter or in lower cost space. 

I think the last one is the best in my opinion.  I have a prototype in https://github.com/ros-navigation/navigation2/pull/5207 to test. If the shortest path by the turning radius really does involve doing that, maybe we should let it. However, if it happens due to refinements for cost weighting / increasing turning radius, perhaps we should prefer sticking with the original value (or another turning value that's not as extreme) which doesn't increase that count. That makes it still possible to happen, but only if its natural for it to happen and not due to later refinement. I'm finding that most of the time this happens is due to the refinement stage, so this would remove some big percentage of them. I also married it with a check to see if there's a refinement that is less than the original cost (but might be larger than some other refined cost) and uses less segments to use. If its better than original and less directional segments, I think that is the preferable direction over slightly shorter but having 2x direction changes. 

What does everyone think?

fault_phenomenon.title: Local and global costmap ~half cell misalignment when both using the global frame
fault_phenomenon.description:

## Bug report

**Required Info:**

- Operating System:
  - Ubuntu 22.04
- Computer:
  - <!-- Nvidia Jetson Orin, 13th Gen Intel NUC, Ryzen 9 7940-HS -->
- ROS2 Version:
  - ROS2 Iron
- Version or commit hash:
  - 1.2.10
- DDS implementation:
  - Cyclone DDS

#### Steps to reproduce issue
Use a rolling local costmap and a static global costmap. Configure both with the same global frame. Typically:
```
local_costmap:
  local_costmap:
    ros__parameters:
      update_frequency: 5.0
      publish_frequency: 5.0
      global_frame: map
      robot_base_frame: base_link
      rolling_window: true
      trinary_costmap: False
      width: 3
      height: 3
      resolution: 0.1
      robot_radius: 0.8
      use_maximum: true

      plugins: ["sync_layer"]
      sync_layer:
        plugin: "nav2_costmap_2d::StaticLayer"
        map_subscribe_transient_local: True
        map_topic: "/global_costmap/costmap"
        subscribe_to_updates: True
        enabled: True
      always_send_full_costmap: True

global_costmap:
  global_costmap:
    ros__parameters:
      publish_frequency: 1.0
      update_frequency: 5.0
      global_frame: map
      robot_base_frame: base_link
      robot_radius: 0.8
      resolution: 0.1
      track_unknown_space: False
      use_maximum: true

      plugins: [...]
```

#### Expected behavior
The local and global costmap are perfectly aligned since their sizes are integers, and the rolling costmap center coordinates is also casted to integer (https://github.com/ros-navigation/navigation2/blob/iron/nav2_costmap_2d/src/costmap_2d.cpp#L331).

![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/8da690e8-d8b6-45d1-abf4-5b9bbd79b1eb)

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/798f0c70-bc92-46e3-a09d-aa4262cf9953

#### Actual behavior

In some cases / after some time (still unclear), the rolling local costmap appears slightly shifted (~40% of a cell) with respect to the global costmap.

![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/aced2e80-177d-4a33-85c5-17139119286f)

#### Reproduction instructions

#### Additional information
Issue originally mentioned in #5152

error_logs.text: * I'm suspect in this case of the origin calculation. The motion of the robot is not in discrete cells (continuous), so since we quash the origin change into an `int`, that would tell me there will be some approximation error. I'd check that first thing.

solution_evidence_candidates.text:
This shift is causing issues when our robot drives close to the border of the working area. Due to the shift, the position of the robot can be non-lethal on the global costmap and lethal on the local costmap. In this case, the planner can find a path, but our DWB follower systematically fails with nav2_core::NoValidControl.

As a consequence, I'll have to find a solution (either the root cause or a workaround). But I was hoping to get some insights from a Nav2 expert :-)

Understood, unfortunately I don't have a 'here's the reason' off of the top of my head. I would have to experiment a bit to gain some intuition about what's happening and what impacts the behavior. Personally what I'd start with is checking that its not an issue with visualization just as a starting point. Then:
* I'm suspect in this case of the origin calculation. The motion of the robot is not in discrete cells (continuous), so since we quash the origin change into an `int`, that would tell me there will be some approximation error. I'd check that first thing. 
* One thing in that area that I would test is changing the calculation of `new_grid_ox` to use the continuous coordinates instead of the static casted `int` version. The static casted version of `cell_ox` is needed later in the function, but I'm not sure that the new grid origin information needs to have that approximation applied. 
* I'm interested if we can see it only in the X or Y dimension and make some adjustments with respect to that axis only to see what helps / hurts and if that's related 
* Certainly the X and Y bounds functions you mention in the other ticket are suspect, but if you're not saying that helped with anything, I wouldn't start there.

My off the cuff intuition would be to crutinize the origin since that is what the rest is offset based off of. The grid is a fixed size so unless you count the cells and see when this happen there's a row / column added or missing, then I don't think it has to do with calculating grid bounds, but rather where the grid itself is placed. I think that's the origin or incoming map data alignment related, possibly.

comments.body:
Renamed for specificity - I hope that still meets your intent. Is this something you're going to look into or a report for some developer / maintainer to look into eventually when time or interest allots? 

I also see you mention Iron, have you tested this on something more modern? I don't recall anything that would fix / brought up an issue like this recently, but it is worth checking that we didn't already fix this issue in `main` or `main_humble` (main branch compatible with Humble) so we don't chase our tails

This shift is causing issues when our robot drives close to the border of the working area. Due to the shift, the position of the robot can be non-lethal on the global costmap and lethal on the local costmap. In this case, the planner can find a path, but our DWB follower systematically fails with nav2_core::NoValidControl.

As a consequence, I'll have to find a solution (either the root cause or a workaround). But I was hoping to get some insights from a Nav2 expert :-)

Understood, unfortunately I don't have a 'here's the reason' off of the top of my head. I would have to experiment a bit to gain some intuition about what's happening and what impacts the behavior. Personally what I'd start with is checking that its not an issue with visualization just as a starting point. Then:
* I'm suspect in this case of the origin calculation. The motion of the robot is not in discrete cells (continuous), so since we quash the origin change into an `int`, that would tell me there will be some approximation error. I'd check that first thing. 
* One thing in that area that I would test is changing the calculation of `new_grid_ox` to use the continuous coordinates instead of the static casted `int` version. The static casted version of `cell_ox` is needed later in the function, but I'm not sure that the new grid origin information needs to have that approximation applied. 
* I'm interested if we can see it only in the X or Y dimension and make some adjustments with respect to that axis only to see what helps / hurts and if that's related 
* Certainly the X and Y bounds functions you mention in the other ticket are suspect, but if you're not saying that helped with anything, I wouldn't start there.

My off the cuff intuition would be to crutinize the origin since that is what the rest is offset based off of. The grid is a fixed size so unless you count the cells and see when this happen there's a row / column added or missing, then I don't think it has to do with calculating grid bounds, but rather where the grid itself is placed. I think that's the origin or incoming map data alignment related, possibly.

I finally understood the issue. The coordinates of the origin of my static costmap were not multiple of the costmap resolution. For example:

```
origin:
- 3.05
- -11.05
```

with a costmap resolution of 0.1.

---------------------
**Explanation**

The global costmap gets its origin from the .yaml file loaded. The origin is enforced by the `static_layer`, when calling `resizeMap` (https://github.com/ros-navigation/navigation2/blob/iron/nav2_costmap_2d/plugins/static_layer.cpp#L205). It can be any float value.

However, the local costmap origin will always be located at `(0, 0) + (N, M) * <costmap resolution>` with (N, M) being integers (see https://github.com/ros-navigation/navigation2/blob/iron/nav2_costmap_2d/src/costmap_2d.cpp#L327).

As a consequence, the X/Y distances between the local and global costmap origins are not systematically multiple of the costmap resolution, leading to the observed shift. 

-----------------
**Solution**

I just made sure that the static costmap created by my system uses origin coordinates which are multiple of the costmap resolution.
Does your PR #6028 resolve this?

> Does your PR [#6028](https://github.com/ros-navigation/navigation2/pull/6028) resolve this?

No, it's completely uncorrelated. The local costmap origin coordinates are always cast to integers. So, even if `getSizeInMetersX` gives a value too small by a half cell width, the origin coordinates are floored and the local costmap grid remains aligned with the global costmap grid.

The shift that I reported here occurs when a static costmap is used in the global costmap, loaded by `StaticLayer`. If its origin coordinates have a resolution smaller than the costmap resolution, the shift appears. For example, if the static costmap origin is (- 3.14, -11.06) and the costmap resolution is 0.1, the shifts will be  0.04 (X) and 0.06 (Y) between the local and global costmaps. This is due to the fact that the function [`resizeMap`](https://github.com/ros-navigation/navigation2/blob/main/nav2_costmap_2d/src/costmap_2d.cpp#L111) used by the `StaticLayer` does not floor the new origin coordinates, while the function [`updateOrigin`](https://github.com/ros-navigation/navigation2/blob/main/nav2_costmap_2d/src/costmap_2d.cpp#L350) used by the rolling local costmap periodic update does.

Sorry, this was a quick scan, I understand better. 

Is there any actionable thing we can do here in this case? It sounds like its dependent on the mapping system (though we could update at least SLAM Toolbox to make sure the resolution and origin are full increments). Is this something we can detect on startup with the rolling static layer to give the user a light warning that they may want to adjust their origin?

We could add a warning [here](https://github.com/ros-navigation/navigation2/blob/main/nav2_costmap_2d/plugins/static_layer.cpp#L210) if `new_map.info.origin.position.x` or `new_map.info.origin.position.y` is not a multiple of `new_map.info.resolution` ( `% resolution != 0`).

```
RCLCPP_WARN(logger_, "StaticLayer: Costmap origin coordinates (%f, %f) are not multiple of costmap resolution (%f). The costmap grid won't align with (0, 0)")
```

Alternatively, we could cast the origin coordinates in `resizeMap` [here](https://github.com/ros-navigation/navigation2/blob/main/nav2_costmap_2d/src/costmap_2d.cpp#L116):
```
origin_x_ = static_cast<int>(origin_x / resolution) * resolution;
origin_y_ = static_cast<int>(origin_y / resolution) * resolution;
```
> Is this something we can detect on startup with the rolling static layer to give the user a light warning that they may want to adjust their origin?

The misalignment only occurs when the StaticLayer receives a new static costmap, at runtime. I don't see any way to predict this at startup.

Ok. I don’t think we should change the origin since many users have annotations and zones based on those coordinates. But we can warn about the misalignment. 

Can you open a PR for that? Though for the message, I would mention about misalignment with rolling and non-rolling grids perhaps?

title: SMAC smoother can generate infeasible paths when using non-circular robots in very confined spaces

fault_phenomenon.title: SMAC smoother can generate infeasible paths when using non-circular robots in very confined spaces
fault_phenomenon.description:
Following up on https://github.com/ros-navigation/navigation2/issues/4271#issuecomment-2879364973

The SMAC smoother could result in an infeasible (colliding) path. The reason is because after modifying the path, it does simple cell cost collision checking (rejects path if cell cost > MAX_NON_OBSTACLE) but does not check for potential collision of orientated footprints.

code_and_log_blocks.text:
cd <nav2_ws>

git -C src/navigation2 fetch https://github.com/MobiusRoamer/navigation2.git fix/smac-smoother-footprint-5330
git -C src/navigation2 checkout FETCH_HEAD

colcon build \
  --symlink-install \
  --packages-select nav2_smac_planner \
  --cmake-args -DBUILD_TESTING=ON

source install/setup.bash

./build/nav2_smac_planner/test/test_smoother \
  --gtest_filter='SmootherTest.rejects_non_circular_footprint_collision'

comments.body: I want to work on this if possible. I haven't examined the code yet, but I know that there is a collision checker built into nav2. Could we potentially use that function here?

The issue here is that we don't have the feasibility information in the smoother currently. So, there'd have to be a check on the feasibility constraints to then be able to get the orientation information (theta) needed to check the footprint. We cannot check the footprint without X,Y,Theta for a pose since the footprint is orientation-dependent when non-circular.

So, we'd probably want to start off by estimating the orientation with the `updateApproximatePathOrientations` function to get an orientation for introducing the collision checker. Then we'd have the X,Y,Theta for each pose to use a collision checker object with (Nav2 Costmap 2D has one of these you can use, see Hybrid-A* NodeT for an example use). 

Then, perhaps trying to do one step better by either changing the way the smoother works to retain orientation information so we know its 'real' or make sure we maintain minimum turning radius constraints so that the computed orientation is known to be drivable. That way if not just collision free, but also doesn't possibly violate constraints (which is rare and not usually a big deal, but can happen and would impact vehicles like Ackermann that have an actual, strict limit)

Hi! I’d like to work on this issue as my first PR.

From the discussion, the main problem seems to be the lack of orientation information in the smoother’s collision check, which only uses simple cell cost and ignores the robot’s oriented footprint.

I’ve reviewed the smac_smoother.cpp code and the issue discussion, and I see that the smoother currently **only checks collisions based on cell costs from the costmap**. This approach doesn’t account for the robot’s oriented footprint, which is critical for non-circular robots in confined spaces.

To address this, I plan to: 

(Use the existing updateApproximatePathOrientations function to estimate the orientation for each pose in the smoothed path. With the (X, Y, Theta) data available, integrate Nav2’s footprint collision checker (similar to how it’s used in the Hybrid-A* planner) to validate the path.)

-> Integrate Nav2’s footprint collision checker into the smoother.

 -> After smoothing and updating the path orientations (x, y, theta), run a footprint collision check on every pose along the path.

  -> If any footprint collision is detected, reject the smoothed path and revert to the last valid path.

   -> Ensure this addition works seamlessly with the existing smoothing logic and does not degrade performance.

I’ll also add tests to verify that the smoother no longer produces infeasible paths due to footprint collisions.

I’d love to work on this as my first PR. Could I please get a go-ahead? Also, any guidance on best practices for initializing the collision checker or existing test cases to build on would be greatly appreciated!

Possible reference: https://github.com/ros-navigation/navigation2/pull/6081, the PR was closed because it's fully AI-generated and not tested

Hi I'd like to have a crack at this as I see previous PRs have closed and no assignees. Had a look at the previous attempts and feedback. Will keep these in mind: preserve the path length and goal pose, avoid unrelated changes, determine the collision handling behaviour before implementation, avoid dup and expensive checks. 

Before opening a PR i plan to reproduce the issue locally and check behaviour with a non-circular footprint in simulation (will probs keep these documented for reproduction in draft pr comments). Will also provide regression tests and document before / after evidence. 

Would it be okay for me to take this on?
Please, we'd love that! I'd say before opening a PR, keep us apprised on your progress and when you think you found the problem for us to chat about :-)

> Please, we'd love that! I'd say before opening a PR, keep us apprised on your progress and when you think you found the problem for us to chat about :-) Thanks! I first tried adding a regression test to show the failure mode. The test builds an unsafe path, but the smoother reports success. The strategy is not to pass an already colliding path to the smoother and expect it to fail, because that would be blending (a) upstream planner or caller giving sth invalid with (b) smoother not rejecting that invalid input, while we just want to isolate (b). So instead I tried: valid input path -> SMAC smoother changes the path -> changed path becomes colliding -> smoother still returns success Here is the added test: https://github.com/MobiusRoamer/navigation2/commit/bfb75f13 To visualize the footprint geometry a bit, `r` denotes the robot centre, ` ```text 1.2m * 0.4m [===========] [ r ] [===========] ^ center ``` X is our obstacle in the following landscape ```text y ^ | 12m r----r----r----r----r----r | | | | X obstacle around (3.1, 11.7), not to scale | | | 10m r | | | 8m r | | | 6m r | | | 4m r | | | 2m r | +--------+----+----+----+----+----+----> x 2m 4m 6m 8m 10m 12m 14m ``` See test results at end of this post. Before smoothing, every original pose is valid. I checked them using `footprint_checker.footprintCostAtPose()`. Then after smoothing, smoother moves poses between the two arms of the `L` corner, one pose gets close enough that its rectangle overlaps obstacle. The bot centre is still not on the lethal X cell, so the old centre cell check passes. But the rectangular footprint at that pose overlaps the obstacle, so the full footprint check fails. My planned fix direction is to validate the full oriented footprint during smoothing, reject an update that introduces a footprint collision, roll back to the last valid path, and return false. Does this direction match what you would expect? fault_phenomenon.title: MPPI acceleration constraints not respected
fault_phenomenon.description:
## Bug report

I have a suspicion that the acceleration limits are not working after https://github.com/ros-navigation/navigation2/pull/5266



#### Steps to reproduce issue

```
ax_max: 0.1
ax_min: -0.1
```

Scenario: some setup that makes your robot accelerate in a straight line

Checkout before and after the PR

#### Expected behavior

See a curve that roughly respects the acceleration constraints


#### Actual behavior

Does not seem to respect the acceleration constraints

#### Reproduction instructions

#### Additional information

code_and_log_blocks.text:
ax_max: 0.1
ax_min: -0.1

solution_evidence_candidates.text:
I decided that is was better to revert, if it breaks acceleration constraints then it is an invalid option as acceleration constraints are super important to be respected. I consider that to be buggy behavior that needs to be fixed before its possible parameterization, I hope you understand. 

> Isn't the control sequence = previous control sequence shifted by one place + noise ?

Yes, but something seems wrong in this case. 

> Also, why is applyConstraints() [only applied to the optimal control](https://github.com/ros-navigation/navigation2/blob/main/nav2_mppi_controller/src/optimizer.cpp#L339)? Shouldn't it be applied in MotionModel::predict()?

It is applied in both.

comments.body: I will go ahead and take on the revert / parameterization action so that this is not delayed. @chanhhoang99  - but I'd love your thoughts.

> @tonynajjar what are you plotting to get those results you posted in #5266?

Oops forgot to mention, that's just linear velocity. The path is straight
But.... what _is_ it 🙃 Position, velocity, Y axis time or motion axis?

Y-axis: cmd_vel.linear.x
X-axis: time

does that answer you?

@SteveMacenski ,
It's okay to revert it. To be honest, I believe I have not yet tested all the case(we do not have the methodology and deep enough understanding to verify such breaking changes).
About the accel limit constrain is not respect, I believe it's an intended output of the PR.
Imagine we are trying to control a robot with a hard accel constrain(I clamped the velocity on my driver controller at a max = 0.5), so as we control the robot, let's say robot is rotating at 1.0rad/s^2, so it takes 1 second to reach 0rad/s. So we as the controller, we need to stop it sooner than expect.
This behavior, I think matches with the predict function, the MPPI prediction must stop it beforehand like we do with teleop_keyboard. So that's why MPPI produce such a steep velocity, but later it will be clamp by the driver.

@SteveMacenski Are you also working on a PR to make this parameterized? Or would you like a contribution?
Even with the oscillations, this is quite helpful for our slow vehicle, so it will be great to have an option.

I would like to keep discussing this change and whether we can make it work. Shall we keep it here?

> Imagine we are trying to control a robot with a hard accel constrain(I clamped the velocity on my driver controller at a max = 0.5), so as we control the robot, let's say robot is rotating at 1.0rad/s^2, so it takes 1 second to reach 0rad/s. So we as the controller, we need to stop it sooner than expect.

@chanhhoang99 but shouldn't MPPI take that into account in the prediction? If it knows the acceleration limit, and can predict for 1second?
Could you also point me to a theoretical basis for this change? Is it https://val-sagrario.github.io/Dynamics%20of%20First%20Order%20Systems%20for%20game%20devs%20-%20Jan%202020.pdf ?

---------

> How would you explain this given we [apply acceleration constraints to the output optimal control](https://github.com/ros-navigation/navigation2/blob/main/nav2_mppi_controller/src/optimizer.cpp#L312-L337), regardless of the motion model? That should ensure no matter what (though quality variable) it should meed the dynamic/kinematic limitations. Is `IDX=0` somehow jumping illegitimately - I don't see any other way?

@SteveMacenski 
I also don't get it. It should all be limited based on `control_sequence_.vx(0)`. Isn't the control sequence  = previous control sequence shifted by one place + noise ?

Also, why is `applyConstraints()` [only applied to the optimal control](https://github.com/ros-navigation/navigation2/blob/main/nav2_mppi_controller/src/optimizer.cpp#L339)? Shouldn't it be applied in `MotionModel::predict()`?
It also only affects `control_sequence_.wz` for `idx >= 1` for some reason.

I decided that is was better to revert, if it breaks acceleration constraints then it is an invalid option as acceleration constraints are super important to be respected. I consider that to be buggy behavior that needs to be fixed before its possible parameterization, I hope you understand. 

> Isn't the control sequence = previous control sequence shifted by one place + noise ?

Yes, but something seems wrong in this case. 

> Also, why is applyConstraints() [only applied to the optimal control](https://github.com/ros-navigation/navigation2/blob/main/nav2_mppi_controller/src/optimizer.cpp#L339)? Shouldn't it be applied in MotionModel::predict()?

It is applied in both.

@adivardi ,

> @chanhhoang99 but shouldn't MPPI take that into account in the prediction? If it knows the acceleration limit, and can predict for 1second?
Could you also point me to a theoretical basis for this change? Is it https://val-sagrario.github.io/Dynamics%20of%20First%20Order%20Systems%20for%20game%20devs%20-%20Jan%202020.pdf ?

You can test this change this way: 
- Try to clamp your vehicle with a really low accel constrain like az_max=0.1 rad/s^2, ax_max=0.1rad/s(Do this with ros2_control or your custom controller node that clamp every cmd_vel sent to the  motor driver to a specific accel constrain you want.). 
- Try yourself to control your vehicle with teleop_keyboard to see how hard it is to control with such constrain.
- Then use the change in this PR, change the az_max and ax_max in navigation MPPI parameter to the same value you clamp on your driver controller(e.g 0.1rad/s^2 and 0.1m/s^2). From my testing, MPPI is still able to control  the vehicle which is really hard to control by teleop_keyboard, which I think the MPPI already takes into account the accel constrain you set in the driver controller.

The link above is not related to this PR. Sorry for the confusion.

> > Also, why is applyConstraints() [only applied to the optimal control](https://github.com/ros-navigation/navigation2/blob/main/nav2_mppi_controller/src/optimizer.cpp#L339)? Shouldn't it be applied in MotionModel::predict()?
> 
> It is applied in both.

Could you please point me to where it is done? I really can't find it.
Only place I find `motion_model_->applyConstraints(...)` is in `Optimizer::applyControlSequenceConstraints()`,  called from `Optimizer::updateControlSequence()`, which is at the end of `Optimizer::optimize()` (after all the critics were evaluated)

[This block](https://github.com/ros-navigation/navigation2/blob/main/nav2_mppi_controller/src/optimizer.cpp#L312-L337) sets the acceleration limits for the optimal trajectory before outputting. The [motion model](https://github.com/ros-navigation/navigation2/blob/main/nav2_mppi_controller/include/nav2_mppi_controller/motion_models.hpp#L85-L95) does so for the sampled input control velocities to create the vehicle velocities at the start.

#### Expected behavior

The optimal and candidate trajectories become very unstable - not sure what's happening internally

#### Actual behavior

Stable trajectories and simple acceleration limiting as if done by the velocity_smoother

#### Reproduction instructions

#### Additional information

error_logs.text: I don’t intuit a reason why in a single iteration that would cause a slower trajectory or why when iteratively run it would result in that either, unless some critic is sensitive to acceleration or there’s a min/max use error when applying the limits so that in some case the 1 is being used when it should be the 5.

comments.body:
A couple of question:
- Related to https://github.com/ros-navigation/navigation2/issues/5464? 
- If you set it to -0.2 - 0.2 or -2.0 - 2.0 do you see an issue? Just making sure its not an issue with fast or slow accelerations themselves and it has to do with asymmetry. Note that the PR #5464 takes issue with was in response to supporting slower acceleration profiles in a more stable fashion if you read its original ticket thread 
- What is the behavior that you see and is this using the motion model changes from 5464?

> Related to https://github.com/ros-navigation/navigation2/issues/5464? No, it reproduces without https://github.com/ros-navigation/navigation2/pull/5266 > If you set it to -0.2 - 0.2 or -2.0 - 2.0 do you see an issue? Just making sure its not an issue with fast or slow accelerations themselves and it has to do with asymmetry. It's because of the asymmetry, similar values work fine, no matter how small or large > this using the motion model changes from 5464? No, without > What is the behavior that you see? It looks like the bigger the difference between ax_min and ax_max, the "shorter" the candidate trajectories are ax_max = 1.0 ax_min= -1.0: ax_max = 1.0 ax_min= -5.0:

Ok. Last question: do you see this with Nav2 on main without your custom changes to solidly mark this as a bug independent of your changes? I don’t have an immediate explanation other than perhaps the wrong acceleration is being used in the wrong place which is uncovering a bug independent how we apply acceleration in the motion model or the post-optimization clamping to make sure optimal trajectories are remaining within dynamic limits. 

I don’t intuit a reason why in a single iteration that would cause a slower trajectory or why when iteratively run it would result in that either, unless some critic is sensitive to acceleration or there’s a min/max use error when applying the limits so that in some case the 1 is being used when it should be the 5.

> do you see this with Nav2 on main without your custom changes

I tried on the latest main now with no changes in MPPI package and still reproduces. It would be useful if anyone else using MPPI could confirm this independently (@doisyg do you use considerably different ax_max and ax_min?), maybe I missed something particular in my setup.
That's enough for me to put this on my queue to look at, thank you. Though help from others are welcome, it might be a few weeks before I can address in earnest

---
### Fixing SMAC Planner Parameter Declaration Issue

I'll fix the crash when dynamically changing the `smooth_path` parameter by moving the SmootherParams declaration outside the conditional block in both SMAC planners.

**Todo List:**
- [x] Find SMAC Planner files (Hybrid A* and State Lattice)
- [x] Read current configure method implementations
- [x] Move SmootherParams declaration outside if condition in Hybrid A*
- [x] Move SmootherParams declaration outside if condition in State Lattice  
- [x] Run build/lint checks if available
- [x] Commit changes and provide PR link

**Changes Made:**

Both files now declare SmootherParams outside the `if (smooth_path)` condition, ensuring parameters are always available for dynamic reconfiguration:

**smac_planner_hybrid.cpp:276-281** and **smac_planner_lattice.cpp:233-238** now use:
```cpp
// Initialize path smoother
SmootherParams params;
params.get(node, name);
if (smooth_path) {
  _smoother = std::make_unique<Smoother>(params);
  _smoother->initialize(...);
}
```

This prevents the `ParameterModifiedInCallbackException` when dynamically toggling `smooth_path` from false to true.

**Completed:** Changes committed to branch `claude/issue-5472-20250821_184253` (commit aeaa8e0).

fault_phenomenon.title: MPPI navigation regression from 1.1.17 to 1.1.18 on Humble
fault_phenomenon.description:
## Bug report

**Required Info:**

- Operating System:
  - Ubuntu 22.04 LTS
- Computer:
  - Intel i7-10700TE
- ROS2 Version:
  - ROS2 Humble binaries
- Version or commit hash:
  - 1.1.18
- DDS implementation:
  - Cyclone DDS

#### Steps to reproduce issue
Create a global path with a cusp.

MPPI config:
```
controller_server:
  ros__parameters:
    controller_frequency: 10.0
    use_sim_time: False
    min_x_velocity_threshold: 0.001 
    min_theta_velocity_threshold: 0.001
    failure_tolerance: 0.3
    odom_topic: /odometry/filtered
    progress_checker_plugin: "progress_checker"
    goal_checker_plugins: ["stopped_goal_checker"]
    controller_plugin_types: ["nav2_mppi_controller::MPPIController"]
    controller_plugins: ["FollowPath"]
    progress_checker:
      plugin: "nav2_controller::PoseProgressChecker" 
      required_movement_radius: 0.25
      required_movement_angle: 0.25
      movement_time_allowance: 20.0
    general_goal_checker:
      plugin: "nav2_controller::SimpleGoalChecker"
      stateful: True
      xy_goal_tolerance: 0.08
      yaw_goal_tolerance: 0.05
    stopped_goal_checker:
      plugin: "nav2_controller::StoppedGoalChecker"
      trans_stopped_velocity: 0.01
      rot_stopped_velocity: 0.01 
      xy_goal_tolerance: 0.08
      yaw_goal_tolerance: 0.05
    FollowPath:
      plugin: "nav2_mppi_controller::MPPIController"
      time_steps: 56
      model_dt: 0.1
      batch_size: 10000
      vx_std: 0.2
      vy_std: 0.0
      wz_std: 0.15
      vx_max: 0.8
      vx_min: -0.5
      vy_max: 0.0
      wz_max: 0.3
      iteration_count: 1
      prune_distance: 4.0
      transform_tolerance: 0.1
      temperature: 0.3
      gamma: 0.015
      motion_model: "DiffDrive"
      visualize: False
      reset_period: 1.0 # (only in Humble)
      TrajectoryVisualizer:
        trajectory_step: 5
        time_step: 3
      max_robot_pose_search_dist: 5.0 # Costmap size / 2
      enforce_path_inversion: True 
      inversion_xy_tolerance: 0.2
      inversion_yaw_tolerance: 0.2
      AckermannConstrains:
        min_turning_r: 0.5
      critics: [
          "ConstraintCritic",
          "GoalCritic",
          "GoalAngleCritic",
          "ObstaclesCritic",
          "PathAlignCritic",
          "PathFollowCritic",
          "PathAngleCritic",
        ]
      ConstraintCritic:
        enabled: true
        cost_power: 1
        cost_weight: 5.0
      GoalCritic:
        enabled: true
        cost_power: 1
        cost_weight: 7.0
        threshold_to_consider: 1.4
      GoalAngleCritic:
        enabled: true
        cost_power: 1
        cost_weight: 3.0
        threshold_to_consider: 0.5
      ObstaclesCritic:
        enabled: true
        cost_power: 1
        repulsion_weight: 1.5
        critical_weight: 20.0
        consider_footprint: false
        collision_cost: 10000.0
        collision_margin_distance: 0.2
        near_goal_distance: 0.5
        inflation_radius: 3.9 # (only in Humble)
        cost_scaling_factor: 1.5 #! 10.0 # (only in Humble)
      PathAlignCritic: 
        enabled: true
        use_path_orientations: true
        cost_power: 1
        cost_weight: 9.0
        max_path_occupancy_ratio: 0.05
        trajectory_point_step: 4
        threshold_to_consider: 0.5
        offset_from_furthest: 4
      PathFollowCritic:
        enabled: true
        cost_power: 1
        cost_weight: 10.0
        offset_from_furthest: 5
        threshold_to_consider: 1.4
      PathAngleCritic:
        enabled: true
        cost_power: 1
        forward_preference: False
        mode: 2
        cost_weight: 2.0
        offset_from_furthest: 20
        threshold_to_consider: 1.4
        max_angle_to_furthest: 0.25
```

#### Expected behavior
The robot can follow the global plan and change direction at cusp points. 

#### Actual behavior
On [1.1.17](https://github.com/ros-navigation/navigation2/releases/tag/1.1.17), the robot properly decelerated before the cusp point, reoriented smoothly, and continued to the goal. I created a YouTube video to demonstrate the expected behaviour with the 1.1.17 version. [Link](https://youtu.be/Vg3p9Pl9L7s)

On [1.1.18](https://github.com/ros-navigation/navigation2/releases/tag/1.1.18 ), the robot stops before the cusp, and a recovery is needed to reach the goal. I also made a video to show [this](https://youtu.be/0O8cqNBuTvA).


#### Reproduction instructions
We updated one of our robots from 1.1.17 to 1.1.18, and the robot's navigation changed drastically for the worse.

title: [RPP] min_distance_to_obstacle and velocity_scaled_lookahead dont work well together when min_lookahead < min_distance_to_obstacle

fault_phenomenon.title: [RPP] min_distance_to_obstacle and velocity_scaled_lookahead dont work well together when min_lookahead < min_distance_to_obstacle
fault_phenomenon.description:
## Bug report

**Required Info:**

- Operating System:
    - Ubuntu 24.04
- Computer:
  - Intel Twin Lake N150, 8GB RAM
- ROS2 Version:
  - Jazzy installed via deb packages
- Version or commit hash:
  - 1.3.8-1noble.20250915.220228
  - Custom RPP with min_distance_to_obstacle from Rolling implemented
- DDS implementation:
  - Zenoh

#### Expected behavior

When using `min_distance_to_obstacle`, I would expect the robot to stop when an obstacle is detected within this range and remain stationary until the path is clear. The collision checking logic should consistently enforce this safety distance, even when the robot's velocity is zero.

#### Actual behavior

The robot initially stops correctly at the specified `min_distance_to_obstacle`. However, it then begins to slowly "creep" forward in a stop-and-go pattern, gradually getting closer to the obstacle and not maintaining the intended safety gap.
I've observed this same creeping pattern in two different scenarios:

1) When using a custom modification to the controller that commands zero velocity on imminent collision.
2) When using the default controller behavior that triggers a Wait recovery on the BT.

#### Steps to reproduce issue

1. Configure the RPP controller with the following parameters, ensuring `min_lookahead_dist` is smaller than `min_distance_to_obstacle`:

```yaml
use_collision_detection: true 
use_velocity_scaled_lookahead_dist: true
min_distance_to_obstacle: 0.65
min_lookahead_dist: 0.2 
```

2. Run a navigation task, and put an obstacle on the robot's path.

3. The robot will approach the obstacle, stop correctly at the `min_distance_to_obstacle`, but then slowly creep closer to it.

#### Additional information

In [isCollisionImminent](https://github.com/ros-navigation/navigation2/blob/ed0d59ff8ffd72631620a1a81c60e2d69c0d14eb/nav2_regulated_pure_pursuit_controller/src/collision_checker.cpp#L114C1-L116), the simulation distance is limited by `carrot_dist`, which shrinks to `min_lookahead_dist` when stopped. This prevents the checker from evaluating the full `min_distance_to_obstacle` range.

```cpp
if (hypot(curr_pose.position.x - robot_xy.x, curr_pose.position.y - robot_xy.y) > carrot_dist) {
    break;
}
```

 **A potential fix that I've tested locally:**

To ensure the simulation always respects the safety margin, the distance boundary can be modified to account for `min_distance_to_obstacle`. This can be done by defining a new limit before the loop:

```cpp
double simulation_distance_limit = std::max(carrot_dist, params_->min_distance_to_obstacle);
```

And updating the break condition to use this new limit:
```cpp
if (hypot(curr_pose.x - robot_xy.x, curr_pose.y - robot_xy.y) > simulation_distance_limit) {
    break;
}
```

This change was tested on a physical robot and resolved the creeping behavior, with no observed negative side effects on general navigation.

I'm opening this issue to report the behavior and share my findings. I'm not sure if the current interaction is the intended design, but this approach seems to make the feature more reliable. I'm curious to hear your thoughts.

error_logs.text: That seems reasonable, but would you think it would also be reasonable to say that the `min_distance_to_obstacle` must be greater than or equal to the minimum lookahead distance? If we say this, we can check this on Configuration / Dynamic Configuration and throw an exception or reject the dynamic update if violated.

My bad, I phrased that poorly. By default RPP throws an exception, which is fine. For our specific use case, we wanted the robot to just stop and wait if it encounters an obstacle. Since in the BT we were basically just triggering thw wait recovery and calling RPP again, I thought it was reasonable to make a local modification for it to just publish a zero velocity instead of throwing an exception.
> I thought it was reasonable to make a local modification for it to just publish a zero velocity instead of throwing an exception.
Isn't a zero sent though in the catching of that exception at the server level before being returned to the BT?

---

> the distance boundary can be modified to account for min_distance_to_obstacle

That seems reasonable, but would you think it would also be reasonable to say that the `min_distance_to_obstacle` must be greater than or equal to the minimum lookahead distance? If we say this, we can check this on Configuration / Dynamic Configuration and throw an exception or reject the dynamic update if violated. 

Do you want to have the minimum distance smaller than the minimum lookahead? 

@doisyg this is related to something you added - FYI. Any feedback you want to provide?

Thanks for the quick reply!

> Is that not in RPP already? If not, can you please open a PR to add that if you found a gap?

My bad, I phrased that poorly. By default RPP throws an exception, which is fine. For our specific use case, we wanted the robot to just stop and wait if it encounters an obstacle. Since in the BT we were basically just triggering thw wait recovery and calling RPP again, I thought it was reasonable to make a local modification for it to just publish a zero velocity instead of throwing an exception.

What I meant is that I observed this "creeping" behavior regardless of how the robot was stopped, whether by my zero velocity modification or by the default using the wait recovery.

> Do you want to have the minimum distance smaller than the minimum lookahead?

I want to have min_distance greater than the min lookahead (in other words, min_lookahead must be smaller than min_distance). 

Basically, I want RPP to stop with a safety margin (like 0.6m - 1.0m), and for that, min_distance seems appropriated. At the same time, I need to keep min_lookahead small, because if I increase it too much, the robot starts to cut corners excessively.

I'm not sure if this is the intended use for the parameter. I'm kind of new to navigation, so please take this with a pinch of salt. Based on my use case, a constraint like this:

> but would you think it would also be reasonable to say that the min_distance_to_obstacle must be greater than or equal to the minimum lookahead distance? 

would actually be problematic, as I would have to choose between having this safety margin or a good path tracking. It seems difficult to achieve both with that constraint.

> I thought it was reasonable to make a local modification for it to just publish a zero velocity instead of throwing an exception.

Isn't a zero sent though in the catching of that exception at the server level before being returned to the BT? 

OK! Can you open that PR? :-)

> Isn't a zero sent though in the catching of that exception at the server level before being returned to the BT?

😳 Ah, I didn't know about that, thanks for the info!

I've opened the PR #5598. I saw some checks are failling, will soon get to it.

On a related note, I was thinking: would it be helpful to add a small note to RPP docs clarifying that min_distance_to_obstacle is a parameter exclusive to rolling? Or is it fine to leave it as is, since the docs track the rolling branch?
The docs track the rolling branch so that’s ok for now. Its not ideal, but its where the docs are at

> There should be no backward motion at the beginning of the route.

Why not? 

It looks like that is the shortest path, by doing that maneuver, it sets itself up at a better orientation in order to make the turn and then fluidly go into the analytic expansion. It probably does help with being the shortest path.

Why do I think it is a bug?  
1. Because whenever the target point is behind the starting point, the path starts by retreating one step.  
2. In the vast majority of scenarios, it only retreats one step.  
This is a very strange behavior, so I believe it is a bug.

It may not be `std::numeric_limits<unsigned int>::max()`, but more likely it is 0. If I want to fix this issue, I can set it to `std::numeric_limits<unsigned int>::max()` in the constructor.  
2. There is also a question about the `getTraversalCost` function. This function calculates the cost to reach the child, but why is it using the parent's `_motion_primitive_index`? Is my understanding incorrect?

I believe I’ve figured it out. The getTravelCost function calculates the cost from the parent to the child. However, if it detects that the parent node is the first node and directly returns a constant cost, that behavior is unreasonable. In other words, the expansion cost for the first node is incorrect. Therefore, to fix this issue, I need to remove the handling logic for the “first node.” After removing it, I tested the change and achieved the expected results.

Is my understanding correct?
Test it out and let me know 😉 Make sure to look at the operations happening after this one. Is anything there using the parent's information that may or may not exist given that it is the first node?

> Test it out and let me know 😉 Make sure to look at the operations happening after this one. Is anything there using the parent's information that may or may not exist given that it is the first node?



After removing the code related to the “first node” check, I didn’t find any parts of the remaining getTravelCost logic that were affected. I also tested various scenarios, including:

   1) When the goal point is in front of the robot — everything works normally.

   2)  When the goal point is behind the robot — this case now also behaves correctly, no longer showing the issue where the robot first moves backward and then moves forward.

   3) When the goal and start positions are the same — the generated path contains only one point, and no abnormalities occur.

Here are some of my observations and understanding:

1) Given the current context of this function, removing the “first node” condition doesn’t seem to cause any issues, because getTravelCost is always used by the parent node to evaluate the cost to its child nodes. In this context, all child nodes appear to be non-nullptr. I also tested the case where the start and goal are the same — meaning the final path contains only one point — and no problems occurred.

2) However, considering that getTravelCost might be used in other scenarios in the future, for safety, we can add a check to see whether the child node is nullptr. If it is, we can return a 0 cost. This would prevent potential crashes in situations where a nullptr child node might appear during expansion.

So the final solution would be either:

1) Simply remove the condition related to the “first node,” or

2) Remove the “first node” condition and add a check to determine whether the child node is nullptr. If it is nullptr, return a cost of 0.

In the current situation, I would prefer to choose option 1.

Please open a PR! Glad you found that it works just fine -- we didn't used to have that function formulated in that way so it looks like now that we focus on the child's metdata rather than the parent, this is all OK!

There is a subtle issue that occurs if you remove that first node check. The start node always has a TurnDirection of UNKNOWN since that is what it is default initialized to. This means that the if-else block at https://github.com/ros-navigation/navigation2/blob/main/nav2_smac_planner/src/node_hybrid.cpp#L418-L430  will always drop into the "penalizes wiggling" block whenever the child node is not FORWARD or REVERSE. 

Essentially this results in the first expansion always preferring non-straight motions more so than other expansions. This behavior may be subtle enough that we can ignore it without too much issue. Otherwise we could move the first node check to https://github.com/ros-navigation/navigation2/blob/main/nav2_smac_planner/src/node_hybrid.cpp#L418 so that we don't apply any turning or change penalties on the first expansion.
